imminent

/IM-uh-nent/ — emphasis on first syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Imminent means about to happen very soon.

When the tremors suddenly grew violent, scientists declared an eruption imminent and urged everyone within twenty miles to leave at once.

Example

The sky darkened over the ocean, and the beach guard scanned the horizon—a hurricane was imminent, and she had minutes to evacuate the swimmers.

Imminent is more precise than a plain word like 'coming' because it captures not just that something will happen, but that it's about to happen right now with urgency and certainty.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

forthcoming: Forthcoming means officially due to arrive — a forthcoming album, a forthcoming report — with no claim about how soon. Imminent is all about nearness in time: it means the thing is about to happen within moments or days. A book can be forthcoming for two years; an imminent storm is nearly here.

impending: Impending means hanging over you and drawing close, almost always something unwelcome — impending doom, an impending deadline. Imminent is a notch more immediate and works for good news as well as bad. An impending exam may be next week; an imminent one starts in minutes.

looming: Looming describes something rising up large and threatening as it draws closer, like a storm cloud or a dreaded meeting. Imminent measures pure closeness in time, without the shadow of menace. Graduation can be imminent and joyful; only something that darkens the horizon looms.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

distant: far off in future time

unlikely: probably not going to happen at all

Where it sits · how close it is to happening — possible → expected → approaching → imminent

possible vs. imminent: Rain is always possible on a spring hike, but when thunder cracks directly overhead, a downpour is imminent and the group sprints for shelter.

expected vs. imminent: The ferry was expected sometime that afternoon; only when its horn finally sounded around the headland was its arrival imminent.

approaching vs. imminent: The comet has been approaching for months and is still millions of miles away; nothing about it is imminent, a word reserved for what will happen in the next few moments.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: upon, over, toward (an assimilated form of in- — not the in- that means 'not')

Root — min-

Root — min-: to jut out, project, threaten (Latin minēre)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: characterized by, being in a state of (present-participle-forming)

Put it together

Put it together: Im- (upon, over — careful: this is not the im- that means 'not') + min- (to jut out, project, threaten) + -ent (in a state of) builds the meaning literally: in a state of jutting out over you — like a cliff overhanging your head, about to come down at any moment. The same root gives eminent and prominent, things that 'stick out,' and menace, a threat that looms.

Use the root in a new word: prominent

Use the root in a new word: prominent: The prominent architect designed buildings that stood out for their bold and innovative style.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Imminent is serious, urgent language for something about to happen very soon. Reach for it when time pressure is critical. For something happening later but still ahead, plainer words like 'expected' or 'coming' fit better.
